(ii) Describe a problem that could occur without control of concurrent access. (3)
(iii) Describe how record locks or timestamp ordering manage concurrent access. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Torquay should be in quotes as a string [B1]
Missing join condition: AND Surgery.SurgeryName = Vet.SurgeryName [B1]
(ii) Two users read the same record at the same time [B1]
Each makes a change and saves it [B1]
The second save overwrites the first — a lost update [B1]
(iii) Record lock: a record being edited is locked so others can't change it [B1]
Until the first transaction finishes (or: each transaction gets a timestamp; operations are rejected if they conflict with a later timestamp) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe serialisation and commitment ordering as methods for managing concurrent access. (4)
(ii) Explain why a client-server database is used in a multi-site organisation. (3)
hints: One at a time; order of commit.
questions.solution:
(i) Serialisation: transactions are run so their effect is as if they ran one after another [B1]
So no transaction overlaps another on the same data [B1]
Commitment ordering: transactions are committed in an order that avoids conflicts / deadlock [B1]
Based on dependencies between transactions [B1]
(ii) Single central database, so all sites see consistent, up-to-date data [B1]
Server handles queries, so clients need less processing [B1]
Easier to back up and secure centrally [B1]

questions.prompt:
Zoo(ZooName, Town, Country); AnimalLocation(AnimalID, ZooName, DateArrived, DateLeft) where DateLeft = 01/01/0001 means still there; Animal(AnimalID, IndividualName, Species, DateOfBirth, Sex).
(i) State which is not required for full normalisation: each non-key attribute depends on the key; no non-key dependencies; primary key is one attribute; atomic attributes. (1)
(ii) Write the CREATE TABLE statement for Animal. (3)
(iii) Write a query listing the name and arrival date of every red panda at "Ashdale Park" at any time from 01/04/2020 to 31/05/2020. (7)
(iv) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of adding ZooName to Animal. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Primary key consists of only one attribute [B1]
(ii) CREATE TABLE Animal (AnimalID VARCHAR(10), IndividualName VARCHAR(30), Species VARCHAR(30), [B1]
DateOfBirth DATE, Sex CHAR(1), [B1]
PRIMARY KEY (AnimalID)) [B1]
(iii) SELECT IndividualName, DateArrived [B1]
FROM Animal, AnimalLocation [B1]
WHERE Animal.AnimalID = AnimalLocation.AnimalID [B1]
AND Species = 'Red Panda' AND ZooName = 'Ashdale Park' [B1]

AND (DateLeft >= #01/04/2020# [B1]
OR DateLeft = #01/01/0001#) [B1]
(iv) Advantage: quicker to find current zoo without a join [B1]
Disadvantage: data redundancy / inconsistency, no longer normalised [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Define first, second and third normal form. (3)
(ii) Explain why the Match relation Match(AnimalFemaleID, AnimalMaleID, DateOfMatch, Successful) uses a composite key. (2)
(iii) Explain insertion, deletion and update anomalies with an example. (6)
(iv) Explain why normalised databases are easier to maintain. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 1NF: atomic data, no repeating groups [B1]
2NF: 1NF and no partial dependencies [B1]
3NF: 2NF and no non-key (transitive) dependencies [B1]
(ii) A single attribute can't uniquely identify a match [B1]
The pair (and date) identifies each pairing uniquely [B1]
(iii) Insertion anomaly: can't add data without other unrelated data [B1]
e.g. can't add a new zoo until it has an animal [B1]
Deletion anomaly: deleting a record loses other data [B1]
e.g. removing the last animal removes the zoo's details [B1]
Update anomaly: repeated data must be changed in many places [B1]
e.g. zoo town stored with every animal [B1]
(iv) Each fact stored once [B1]
So updates are made in one place, avoiding inconsistency [B1]
